text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy NX EK-GN120ZKAXAR Galaxy Wireless Smart Android 4G Camera 20.3MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 4.8-Inch LCD with 18-55mm OIS Lens (Black) Just opening the box is a joy, making this a great gift. Instead of the usual plastic and white or brown packing, all is in a beautifully designed chic black, with every item showcased to perfection.
Easy set up, right out of the box. I bought the [[ASIN:B00C7EPVHY Samsung Galaxy Camera with Android Jelly Bean v4.2 OS, 16.3MP CMOS with 21x Optical Zoom and 4.8" Touch Screen LCD (WiFi - White)]]a few months ago (also a great camera if you don't want to mess with a cell service for your camera) so it took no time at all, but even if you're an android newbie, it's still simple and straightforward. The Samsung website has some terrific videos showing various features. After an initial get-to-know-ya with this camera, check out more cool things you can do. Also, I myself find it helpful in the beginning to download the PDF of the manual and print off parts I want. The whole manual is over 200 pages, so I just print off what I need.

And even if you're relatively new to photography you'll feel like a pro with an easy to change lens. And about the lens, WOW! Looking at this camera? Get the model that includes the lens! More about the lens later...I could not be more excited!

The Optical Image Stabilizer in the 18-55mm lens offers clear, sharp images. The NX System lens incorporates i-Function Technology which lets you control the camera from the lens itself. It provides one step control of the shutter speed.
The AF (Auto Focus) is fast at 0.17 (!!!) seconds so it easily catches up to your next shot.
Recently, I was photographing an awards ceremony. The 'money shot', of course, was the transfer of the award. My darn camera took so long to autofocus from the previous shot, I missed it. Got a second before, a second after. That will never happen again.
And this is really cool...put the viewfinder up to your eye, and the touchscreen is disabled so your face isn't interfere with the screen icons.

The GPS tracker enables photographers to capture their exact geographical location in real time.

I'm already picking out the goodies to add to this camera. Samsung has a 10mm Fisheye lens, a 20mm pancake lens for taking great landscapes and an 18-200mm zoom...jeez, too many to mention that can be purchased separately. There are a lot of NX cases on eBay, if you want the 'real' one, when I looked, it was cheaper via Amazon versus the Samsung website.
You can also get external flash, remote switch, microphone.

This is THE camera, and the future of all cameras. It's easy enough for a budding photographer, slick enough for the pro.

Any other questions or anything you WISH this review had, just click the 'comment' button below and I'll do whatever I can to help, be it a video, research, whatever. I love it and am happy to share whatever I can so that you can decide if it's right for you.

UPDATE EDIT 3/4/14: The features and options never seem to end on this camera! It can get complicated, but thankfully Samsung has a dedicated support line for it. I've called twice with questions, never had to wait too long. Because this product is so new, if they don't know what youre talking about, ask to be switched to 'professional camera equipment' NOT 'digital camera'.
I feel like there are no stupid questions, only stupid answers, so I admit I asked some stupid questions. They were explained with enough information that I could look up and research the rest.
Since I am NOT a lifelong camera person, some features that would be 101 to others were new to me. And I'm so glad I had the Galaxy with Android Jelly Bean v4.2 OS, 16.3MP first.
The more I peek into what it can do, the more excited I am. One thing I should clarify about my review...I say it is fine for a budding photographer, and it is, but if you just want something to take photos or movies that is point and shoot, you won't be taking advantage of it's full potential. This is a camera for geeks and tech junkies! If you are a newbie, but have the DESIRE, this can be a first pro camera.
There is nothing else like this out there right now.

Someone asked about a 'zoom button'. Like any professional camera, you zoom with the lens, you WANT to zoom with the lens. Part of what is cutting edge about this camera is the way the lens 'talks' to the camera. The information about the functionality of the lens is sent to the body of the camera, so that any options that you have to control the lens shows up on the screen. Each additional lens you may choose to add has different functionality...screen options CHANGE with each lens because the camera KNOWS which lens is on. This is HUGE!
NEVER has this been done before, and I believe it will change the art of photography.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy NX EK-GN120ZKAXAR Galaxy Wireless Smart Android 4G Camera 20.3MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 4.8-Inch LCD with 18-55mm OIS Lens (Black)

Additionally, the drive gets really hot with use. hot to the touch and almost worrisome. I know this may be somewhat normal for NVME drive enclosures but it definitely feels above my personal safety threshold.

I tend to not follow the advice of "Protect your phone's battery and your charger cable by not using your phone while it's charging!!" What can I say, I'm a rebel. Because of this, my chargers don't last very long. I've had about a week of consistent use for the 4ft version of this one and I am really enjoying it. I have a few pros and one con.
The positives:
-The cable feels incredibly sturdy in your hands. It would take a lot for it to start ripping or breaking.
-I tested the charging capacity with multiple reciprocals to see if it effected the charge. As expected, the charging capacity depends solely on the power it is provided with, which is great!
-The length is manageable without being too much. Anything 6ft or longer tends to be flaky. This 4ft is absolutely fantastic in my opinion.
-The lightning adapter plugs into my phone easier than the Apple branded one that came with my phone so that was a bonus! The ease of plugging in does not effect unplugging, it unplugs just like any other charger and does not fall out.
-The leather strap is personally useless for me since I typically never move my chargers and don't travel, but I still appreciate the accessory. The leather feels durable and the clasp is sturdy. If you are someone who travels frequently or transports your chargers, the strap will make it much more compact and easy.

The negative:
-I hate the visual design. The black with white speckles is supposed to be aesthetically pleasing, but instead it makes the charger look dirty.

All in all, I would say this is a fantastic charger with a great price point. This charger would last much longer than others at similar price points. I will continue to be using this product consistently.

text_fidelity_a:
Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US) Though I am giving a review for this backpack, I can't come from the perspective of having used it for a while. I only received my Targus backpack yesterday, but from the looks of it I am pretty darn sure this backpack will last a long, long time. I've used MANY backpacks in the past carrying books, laptops and supplies during the time it took to earn two separate college degrees, and at my previous job of 17 years. I had to carry tools, manuals, laptops and assorted parts to calibrate monitoring equipment around my state. I was rough on the backpacks and some wore out.

I really wish I had had a backpack like this one. It's very well constructed out of strong materials, has a plethora of pockets and places to organize your stuff, and though I don't have a 17" notebook as of yet, it appears to be deep and wide and should easily fit one. There are even slots for file folders and inside zipper pouches. There are pockets on the inside and pockets on the outside. The bottom inside has a foam rubber "shock pad" that neatly folds down flat on the bottom of the backpack and is about 1/2" thick. Plus the bottom is covered in a waterproof rubbery material that should definitely help keep water from seeping up into the bag. That happened to me several times on my job with my other backpacks and it was really frustrating. It's very easy to set your backpack down on the ground not realizing the area is wet.

The shoulder straps are padded and adjustable, and it has a waist strap for extra stability. Even if you didn't use this backpack to tote your 17" marvel of technology around, it would serve well as a camper/hiker backpack. I can't wait to start using it. If something should go wrong or tear up, I will most definitely update this review telling about it, but for now I can find no fault whatsoever with it.
text_fidelity_b: Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US)

text_fidelity_a:
CanaKit Raspberry Pi 3 Complete Starter Kit - 32 GB Edition This is a very complete kit and does contain everything you need to setup a Raspberry Pi 3. Yes, the op system installs easily and, with luck, you can be up and running in less than an hour. So, why the 2 stars?

It gets 2 stars because the Raspberry Pi is probably one of the most frustrating devices I've ever tried to put to any real use. For example, I wanted to set it up so I could use a VNC server on the Pi and a VNC client on my Mac (OS X El Capitan). After three days of almost non-stop failures, I'm sick of this thing. Researching how to get this task done leads you down a black hole of internet articles and posts on the Raspberry Pi site, most of that give different instructions, use different commands, tell you which files to edit and what to put in them, and almost none work, period!

The core problem rests squarely on the Raspberry Pi organization. Their own website is full of conflicting posts on how to do just about anything beyond a basic setup. Few, if any posts state which model of Pi is being referenced, and many bear no date. All in all, it's a very frustrating experience and, while I like to tinker with these things, a little success is required once in a while to keep me chugging along. I think I'm done with this thing. I had hoped it would finally be a Linux for the rest of us. Unfortunately, it's just as convoluted and difficult to use as any version of Linux out there (my opinion).

However, if you're looking to explore the Pi, this kit has everything you need to do a basic setup of Linux. And, should you want to use it as a web server, file server, media server, you're really on your own. Drink lots of coffee and plan to pull our lots of hair.
text_fidelity_b: CanaKit Raspberry Pi 3 Complete Starter Kit - 32 GB Edition

text_fidelity_a:
SABRENT 7 Port USB 3.0 HUB + 2 Charging Ports with 12V/4A Power Adapter [Black] (HB-U930) This is a nicely design USB hub. It has the two feature I look for first in a hub: a compact footprint, and the ability to plug into the wall without having to deal with a wall wart at the end of the plug. While this does have a transformer, it is an in-line version that doesn't interfere with the plug end.

Installation is the typical plug-and-play that is typical with a USB hub. It includes a USB 3.0 cable, and works very well as a USB 3.0 hub under Win 7. I also tried it on an older USB 2.0 machine running XP and had no problems at all (running, of course, at USB 2.0 speed).

The build quality feels very solid. No problems with ports wiggling around even when I stressed the USB cable far more than in normal use. I’ve used other Sabrent hubs and have yet to have a problem with them, even after dropping them.

The hub includes a base that keeps it well-planted in use.

In addition to using this as a USB hub, it also has 2 charging ports that provide 2A output each. Both worked fine when used to charge a phone and a tablet.

The only quibble I have is that it lacks an on/off switch. Not a big deal, but having a switch can come in handy at times.

Overall, it’s a well-designed and well-built hub with a number of good design features. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a compact 3.0 hub with a lot of ports.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT 7 Port USB 3.0 HUB + 2 Charging Ports with 12V/4A Power Adapter [Black] (HB-U930)

text_fidelity_a:
MavisLink HDMI Cable Fiber Optic 100ft 4K 60Hz HDMI2.0b 18Gbps HDR10 ARC HDCP2.2 YUV4:4:4/4:2:2/4:2:0 Slim Flexible for HDTV/Game Console/Projector/Home Theatre I gave this a four because it did not work on one out of three devices I tried it with (and I know each to work with a short HDMI cable). I'm not sure why this had a lot of flickering when used with my Alienware computer, but it worked perfectly with another computer and my QNAP NAS (worth noting is the NAS puts out a very weak signal and does not work with my in-place 25-ft. traditional HDMI cable).

I had almost written this off because usually HDMI is a crapshoot when it comes to any sort of distance and I didn't even realize such a product existed until I read about fiber optic cable inside. I thought that was a generic brand typo type of situation until I looked this up and realized this is a real thing. I didn't study it, but I gather/assume that there is a chip inside that changes electrical signals to low power lasers to send the signals this way. Interesting, though, because there are not 19 fibers inside (a traditional HDMI cable has 19 pins, I think).

I probably need to research this further just because it's totally cool, but I love this thing because I can now watch my NAS directly on my TV even though it is down in the basement (and there is a great app to act as a remote since I now do not have line of sight for the IR remote). I only took off a star because it apparently has some issues with my one computer - not sure why but if you need a couple of these, you might want to buy one at a time to be sure what it does and does not work with. I love it, but had to remove a star for that reason.
text_fidelity_b: MavisLink HDMI Cable Fiber Optic 100ft 4K 60Hz HDMI2.0b 18Gbps HDR10 ARC HDCP2.2 YUV4:4:4/4:2:2/4:2:0 Slim Flexible for HDTV/Game Console/Projector/Home Theatre

Sony WF-1000XM4 Industry Leading Noise Canceling Truly Wireless Earbud Headphones with Alexa Built-in, Black This product feels different to me than other Sony stuff I've gotten. It's like they've gone out of their way to make everything feel like cardboard. The packaging was like egg carton, and the earbuds and their charging station are a rough lightweight material in a drab color. The earbuds themselves are customizable, but bulky compared to the competition. I find them hard to get out of the container, hard to hold onto, and hard to wear. The noise cancellation and sound are both above average though. I like the charging light on the container. It communicates with color and flashes what the status of the product is, and isn't bright or hard to locate.

USB-C charging makes the base station charge up nice and fast. It holds the earbuds securely, and doesn't rattle or fall open. It's also a nice pocketable size and shape with no sharp corners, making the whole product especially portable. Controls are gesture, rather than button. I'm not a fan of this because I end up doing a lot of swiping and hoping. A click button interface, I can just click it the number of times I know will do what I need, and move on.

I've got a few Sony audio products that I use every day and am very happy with, but with earbuds, I'm sticking with jabra for now. It's a competitive market right now for earbuds. Lots of companies putting out new designs.

ANTOP Omnidirectional HDTV Antenna Smartpass Amplified Outdoor 55/65 Miles Long Range AT-414B I've been collecting random TV antennas for review and from yard sales for years, and I think I've had about a dozen now. I generally only keep the two best ones. I tested this one out against my previous champion, which was just a single heavy duty rabbit ear on a magnetic base that somehow beat bigger, newer, and powered models.

The first thing I did with this when I got it was take it apart. I've gotten some in the past where the big plastic dish parts were just plastic for show and had nothing in them. Inside this one were multiple omnidirectional antennas and a circuit board. After attaching it to the coax, I checked through my channels and noticed I was missing some. I then added in the powered section, but didn't turn it on. This totally switched which channels I was missing. Then I turned it on and I got all my channels, plus another one I hadn't previously gotten, so it wins. The various parts do actually do something.

The pictures don't give much idea of scale. It's about the size of a steering wheel and comes with mounting plate. It's kind of huge and I wasn't pleased when I saw the size, but hey, I'll take the size if I get a brand new channel out of the deal.

I received a sample for review but the opinions are my own.

I wouldn’t use it when I need a heavy duty cool down, but it’s adequate to keep my laptop from running too hot when I’m browsing (I use a lot of tabs) or watching videos.

The fan is pretty quiet, but not silent. If I don’t have any music or videos playing, I can hear it.

The blue light is always on when the fan is plugged in. There is no way to toggle or shut off the light. The laptop blocks most of it, but of course that depends on the size of the laptop.

The underside of the unit is mostly plastic. I wasn’t careful when I picked it up one time and nearly snapped a plastic vent over one of the fans.

What really brings this fan down for me is the USB cord/plug. The cable is short -- it’s about 16 inches long. The way the USB plug is designed limits the whole unit’s usage if the USB ports on your laptop are too close together.

I wanted to try this fan out underneath my mom’s Mac Book Pro. It’s an older model that only has two USB ports, side by side. She has a wireless mouse dongle plugged into one port, and so I’m unable to plug in the fan because the cable is in the way. I’ve included a picture to show what I mean.
text_fidelity_b: FLAGTOP Laptop Fan Cooling Pad with 2 Big Fans, Compatible with 14 - 15 inch Computer, Lightweight, Quiet, Slim, Portable Laptop Cooling Fan with 2 in 1 USB Port, Blue LED Light, Adjustable Stand

text_fidelity_a:
Anker 2.4G Wireless Vertical Ergonomic Optical Mouse, 800 / 1200 /1600 DPI, 5 Buttons for Laptop, Desktop, PC, Macbook - Black Update: I have now tried two other brands (a coworker's, and bought another brand) of ergonomic mice that both work substantially better than the Anker version, which also cost less! I highly suggest anyone considering buying this, skip over it and look for another one that is cheaper with good reviews. It amazes me that a company with a known name can skip out on quality so much that other product that cost half as much outperform it in every way.

The Good:
Feels great to hold. More natural than a typical mouse. All the buttons are in the right places and do not require any strain to press. The wheel is in the perfect spot to be used by my middle finger, which is typically what I try to do, since I swear I already have arthritis in my point finger being under 30 years old...

The Bad: There is an obvious input delay, making this pretty terrible for anyone who grew up using computers. That no one else has mentioned this is beyond me. Side by side comparison of any of my Logitech mice and this Anker mouse makes the input delay on this mouse even more obvious. It feels like trying to use a mouse on a TV with interpolation (120 Hz, smooth motion, etc.) enabled. On top of the nearly deal-breaking latency issue, the input into the computer is inconsistent, causing the mouse to frequently skip around or miss my movements.

If you expect to play any game that requires any amount of precision or is time-based, you will regret buying this mouse. Games aside, this mouse reduces my productivity because of how unreliable the signal is, and the extra effort needed to predict the movement of the cursor due to the lag.

I tried the wired version of this mouse (a friend had it) and the input lag is not as bad, but is still there. Therefore, I advise against anyone buying this or the wired version, and suggest to instead look elsewhere.
text_fidelity_b: Anker 2.4G Wireless Vertical Ergonomic Optical Mouse, 800 / 1200 /1600 DPI, 5 Buttons for Laptop, Desktop, PC, Macbook - Black

Kingston 8 GB Class 4 SDHC Flash Memory Card SD4/8GB I ordered this part for use with a new Audibon Birdcam. The Kingston memory card failed in just over a month. It was unreadable by several PCs and a Mac. Amazon said to contact Kingston directly (Kingston memories carry a lifetime warranty). Kingston had me return the memory (my expense) and issued an RMA. They used "UPS Mail Innovations" to ship.
UPS MI is an el-cheapo service that uses the USPS mid-stream and for final delivery. Predictably, the shipment to me was lost by the USPS and tracking information abruptly stopped. It took four telephone calls to Kingston, the final call being to a supervisor, to get another parts shipped. The CS reps kept reading me the dead tracking info in which the shipment was "out for delivery" in another state and past due by several days. It's been three weeks since I sent the part back. I'm waiting for the second RMA part to arrive.
I'm not sure that Sandisk memories are fundamentally any better, but I can say that I never suffered a failure of any of their many memories I own.
text_fidelity_b: Kingston 8 GB Class 4 SDHC Flash Memory Card SD4/8GB

text_fidelity_a: Pioneer Electronics Audition Series XW_NAS3-K Docking Station for iPod (Black) I was the happy owner of the original Bose sounddock for seven years until it stopped working this November.  I thought that was a very good run.  To replace the Bose I chose the Pioneer NAS3 and waited a month for the price to drop to $220.  I like the clean design as I wasn't looking for a display nor was I looking for an alarm clock.  On first play I was not at all impressed with the muddy flat sound until I found that under the music menu on the ipod is a setting for 'speakers'.  Going into 'speakers' I can enhance the sound with the bass/treble on setting which is comparable to the ipod EQ acoustic setting.  You can really bump up the sound by turning on both but for me the sound becomes unnaturally bright and the bass distorts.  In other words the dock does respond to all ipod EQ settings.  Under 'speakers' I can also set the ipod display to always be on, always be off, or only come on when I press a key on the dock or on the remote.  Speaking of the remote, the range is strangely bad as you need to point it almost directly at the unit.  To make the NAS bluetooth capable then you'll need to buy the adaptor separately.  I don't know if it's only the Pioneer adaptor that will work but if that's the case, it's a pricey option at about $70. If this were an issue for me I would have rated the Pioneer three stars.  The sound quality here just doesn't earn it a five-star rating but I'll be keeping the unit.  If I had it to do it over again I would go with another Bose.
text_fidelity_b: Pioneer Electronics Audition Series XW_NAS3-K Docking Station for iPod (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium) I love my FiiO X5 2nd gen player! I love that it has two micro SD card slots (which I use both for a total of 192GB of storage space, with one 64GB card and one 128GB card), because I can put two separate sets of music in there and go back and forth between the cards depending on my musical needs (for example, on the 64GB card, I put recently purchased tracks, and for the entirety of my rest of my library, I put those tracks on the 128GB card). It allows me faster access to my newer stuff, which I want to listen to now, vs. randomizing the rest of my music from the other card.

The sound is unheard of (ha ha, sorry for the pun). Nothing compares to the quality of sound that comes out of this little machine, for its size and price. Pair it with a set of high quality hi-fi headphones and some FLAC music files, and you've got yourself an insane little music machine. You'll never go back to Apple or another brand of music player. You'll find yourself hooking it up to your home sound system and playing all of your music through it. I can't say enough for the sound quality. You WILL notice a difference between crummy .mp3 files and other low-quality sound files. You WILL find yourself craving FLAC files, and you will go wherever you can to find them. You might even start converting your entire CD music collection into FLAC, even though you'd already converted them all to .mp3. You WILL find yourself hoping that someday soon, Amazon will start offering FLAC files instead of .mp3s! (HINT HINT NUDGE NUDGE!) ;) Seriously, though, you probably haven't realized how GOOD your music will sound until you listen to it on this FiiO X5 2nd gen. Even the .mp3s sound better. Especially if you use noise cancelling headphones.

I like that you can adjust the configuration and tell it which buttons to remain active when the screen is off, depending on your preferences. I also like that there are several preset themes to choose from. The screen is easy to read and nicely displays album art.

The unit itself has a wonderful weight to it given the aluminum shell. The volume wheel moves easily and there is a slight tactile feedback click. That wheel controls both the song volume and song selection, depending on which screen you're on when you use it. The power on button has a tiny LED light that's blue when it's running and red when it's charging. There are volume up/down buttons beneath the power button and those buttons are some of the buttons that you can choose whether or not to have active while the screen is off.

I'm not sure if I there's a firmware update that needs to be done that could change this, but there are a couple of things that are pretty bothersome in general about this unit:

1) There is no way to search for a song. If, like me, you have more than 5,000 songs, it's impossible to sit and scroll through each album/folder to find a specific song. I suppose if you're some kind of major organization guru (which I thought I was, but apparently not at this), it would be possible to arrange your music folders into genres or some other category to make it easier to get to the exact music you need to play, but if you've moved over from iTunes like I have, you're probably real spoiled with the ability to view songs either by artist, album, song name, etc., as well as the ability to do a search. Here, you're pretty much on your own, depending on how you've got your music library set up. Having purchased most of my music here on Amazon, it's all arranged by artist name in individual folders. I have several hundred folders set up like this, and scrolling through everything with that scroll wheel can take a very, very long time to find the one thing you're looking for.

2) The unit can be quite SLOW to respond to your clicks. It is not touch-screen, and when you click on a button to change tracks forward/backward or to change from looking at what's playing into another option, such as a list of the songs on the album, it can be quite sluggish. Again, if you're used to using an iPod, you'll be frustrated with the lack of responsiveness of this unit. Again, I keep hoping a firmware update will come out that addresses this.

3) Whenever you add music to your micro SD card(s) [NOTE: There is NO onboard storage, it's purely on whatever card(s) you insert into it] you have to completely update your whole media library. This can take a long time depending on how much music you have, so keep this in mind and don't expect to add music and listen to it immediately. In other words, plan ahead for this :)

4) It's not as user friendly as the typical Apple products you may be used to. You'll get used to it, but don't expect the polished feel because of issues like #1 and #2, above.

5) Playlists are not straightforward. Yes, you can be playing a song and add it to a playlist that resides on one of your SD cards. However, importing playlists can be tricky and you may find yourself looking to the internet to help convert your existing playlists from your prior player. Expect to spend some time on this unless you're totally okay with starting over from scratch (I wasn't okay with this). Also, any playlists that you save to your SD card that you've hand-converted do not show up as a playlist on the FiiO. Instead, you have to navigate to the file on your player as if you were looking for a song, and play it as if you were playing a song. Only playlists you've created on the machine show up in the Playlist section, not playlists you've brought in from elsewhere. There is no 'import' feature or anything fancy like that, so you're pretty much on your own unless you add a song one at a time to Playlist 1, Playlist 2, etc. (I do not yet see a way to rename these as there is no keyboard function on this machine, so you're stuck with those names).

I think with time, the FiiO's software will catch up closer to what you're seeing from the high-visibility media consumer based music players, but right now with this X5 you should be more concerned with how WONDERFUL your music sounds vs the issues associated with the frumpy software that comes with it.
text_fidelity_b: FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium)

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (4th Gen) | Smart speaker with Alexa | Twilight Blue The spherical Echo Dots do not sit well with the various echo holders. If you are thinking of wall mounting this device you'd do better by buying a small platform/shelf to place it on. The indicator light is on the bottom. This gets hid easily by the various Echo Dot wall mounts. Like all Echo Dots, they are great to control smart devices but get very poor marks in understanding the elderly and those slow of speech. As one who is elderly, wears dentures, and hard of hearing, I don't get my words pronounced with distinction. Echo will usually respond with something it found on the web that has zero relation to what I asked of it. My wife is slow of speech and the echo will cut her off and try to process the fragment without waiting for her to complete. I have submitted a request to Amazon about this to have a final key word to denote end of speech but they have not made any changes to the software, nor replied to my comments.
Overall it is a worthwhile device to have. With as many smart devices that we have to simplify our life this has been a Godsend. However, its impatient teen attention span is annoying when trying to issue commands or to have it actually find something on the web...like we asked.

I don't particularly care about the complaints regarding gigabit limitations etc. When I get fibre with equivalent speeds to my house or need to stream ultra HD some day, then I'll worry about it. In interim, HD video streaming, surfing, gaming etc..all work flawlessly.

Comments for WD PowerLine owners:
1. WD utility is unable to pickup on speed of the TP-Links (Rate Mbps). This is an application issue obviously and not completely sure if I can get around this as of yet.
2. I have not secured or modified network name as of yet which made things easier. Hope this does work when I get to it.
3. Ensure you have space for the bulky plug in unit. Not really an issue if you take the bottom wall plug.

For everyone:
My WD PowerLines were collecting dust until I moved. My previous home had a different circuit setup that prevented any PowerLine units from working correctly. They would see each other, but speeds were like dialup. So, don't be ticked if these do not work.

My new house has limited drops and roughly 3k Sq Ft over 2 floors and have no issues. My WD's have over 160 Mbps indicated on the utility from top to bottom.

Unit ceased communicating with the base unit in November 2021.

Had Energizer Lithium AA cells installed. Changed out to new AA alkaline cells. No communication with base unit.

Changed "A-B-C" channel from "C" to "A". Still no communication.

The unit has no capability of wifi to my phone.

Display is very very bright. Lights up the whole kitchen/living room. May be too bright for some, though there are three levels of brightness.

I think my next weather station will have a predominantly dark display instead of this predominantly bright display. The new device will also connect to my phone.

To its credit, it has operated in impossibly high Arizona desert temperatures where it read 121 degrees. I'm sure the unit itself was hotter as it was sitting in the blistering sun all day for several years.

Still, being a weather station, one would assume it's *designed* to sit out in all manner of weather, no matter how hot or cold.

text_fidelity_a:
Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black My SX280 HS is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 lens errors. This is the closest replacement, AFAIK. The 40x zoom is probably not that useful, since the 280's 20x was right at the limit of stable framing, but no biggie. I just like the SX HS series with the DIGIC 6 processor. I looked at the 730, but didn't need Bluetooth & didn't like the look of the oversimplified controls. And $50 buys a couple of extra batteries.

One thing you do get for several years of technology development is a better battery/sensor. Thus far the 720 shows no sign of gobbling electricity the way the 280 does. The extra $100 also buys a better written manual. I discovered a couple of minor features both cameras have, but which you'd be hard pressed to figure out from the 280's manual.--9/2/2017
Update: The 280's video/battery life problems are fixed in the 720. Image stabilization is very good. I got acceptable results at >20x zoom with a light-weight monopod (a Slik). Close focus also appears much better.--9/4/2017
I'm still on my first battery charge!--9/17/2017
Update: I fixed the 280's lens errors with a can of air and a heavy hand blowing out the gaps in the lens. Risky, but it worked. The 720 is still my go to camera. I upped the rating to 5.
July 2019 Update--I got a killer deal on a Panasonic Lumix ZS70. Great camera ... but ... it feels a lot bigger than this one in my hand. It has more features, does more things, but the 720 is lighter, handier, and in some cases takes better still pictures. If you don't need an EVF, tilt-screen and better video, this (or its SX740HS successor) might just be the better choice. The 740 has a tilt-screen.
June 2020
One word of advice. The sensor is 20 Mpx. The lens is capable of delivering 5-8 Mpx. This is typical of these small cameras. Don't be afraid to use lower resolutions or higher compressions. You won't lose much. Still a favorite camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation This is a great streaming box! Like the title says, it's a ROKU on steroids. I have an Apple Airport Extreme router and the ROKU would "occasionally" start buffering because of the processor; however, with the Amazon Fire TV, that's not an issue because it has a quad-core processor. Great streaming box!

Updated 5-4-14 I've had the Fire TV for a couple of months now and for the most part it's great; however, today we rented "Bad Grandpa" on Amazon. It played great but when there was 35 mins left in the movie, it quit playing. Tried to restart the movie and got a message saying there was a problem with playing the movie and to contact Amazon Customer Service. I called them and they said that when this happens, "...unplug the Fire TV for 15 seconds and then plug it back in." In my opinion, that takes the fun out of watching a movie! I thought the memory and quad-core processor would be enough to stop this from happening, wrong! Having said that, instead of naming my review "ROKU on Steroids" I should have named it "Just like ROKU".

The Amazon rep said that it was a problem with the memory of the Amazon Fire TV and not the video. When asked if the problem could be fixed by Amazon with an update, all he said was "I'll forward that to Amazon".

If you don't mind watching videos that stop playing and having to unplug the Fire TV and restart it during a movie, you'll really like the Fire TV.

One other point, the Amazon rep stated that it might be my router. I have an Apple Airport Extreme, the best and fastest available. If it was my router, I guess the Amazon rep should have had me unplug my router instead of the Fire TV. He finally admitted that it was the Fire TV and not the router.

Just wanted to get this information out there so people can be informed about the Amazon Fire TV before purchasing one. All in all, I'm happy with the Fire TV...just aggravated that I have to unplug it and restart it when watching movies. The Amazon Fire TV should be better than this!
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation

Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model) 7 May 2014: Thanks to Google's omission of full USB OTG function, file transfers are frustrating & sometimes impossible. When I return home, I'm rooting it.

After 24 hours, I like it. It's a little different from my Galaxy Player 5 inch. The extra processor speed is nice. So is the combination of the light weight and larger screen. The GP5 was getting bogged down by software bloat. It fits nicely in my old K3 case. So far, so good.

...and it works with my Targus Bluetooth keyboard. Actually, it works better than it does with the GP5. The Samsung has some key-mapping problems, probably due to Gingerbread.

As to reading, I happened to be starting a novel the other day, and started it on the Nexus 7. I had no problem. I did keep the brightness on 'Auto', so the light level of the screen matched the ambient light. With the GP5, matching light levels was a little chancy, so I had a bit more eyestrain. (Of course the extra 2" of screen have no bearing on that, right?)

I did try the freebie 'La Luna' video that Google gives away. It watched fine on the 7" screen. The thing I really like is that there is a 7" screen in the weight of a past-technology 5" package. I owned a Nook color for 13 days, but took it back because of the weight and balance. It just wasn't comfortable to hold.

I haven't tried any significant music listening. I suspect I'll still prefer my Clip+ for that. The Nexus is a little large for that purpose. I also haven't tried the camera in any particular serious way. A selfie and a picture of my cat isn't much of a trial. Again, I'll probably use a purpose-made camera for real pictures. I also haven't explored portability yet. In the case, it's a bit bulky for easy transport, whereas the GP5 fits in my pocket next to my cell phone. I probably won't put the N7 in my pocket without a case. It's a little large and fragile seeming for that.

...As to the camera, it's OK, the image quality is fine, but a 7" tablet just isn't a good ergonomic platform for picture taking. This is the best from an afternoon at Mass Audubon's Ipswich River Wildlife Sanctuary.

Picture is available at:
MobileRead Forums > E-Book Readers > Android Devices>Nexus 7 2013 1st Impressions

...And I still prefer my Clip+ for music. I hand to hunt around the Android store for a decent player for my collection which includes WMAs as well as MP3s. Google does not play WMAs (cue prissy, superior sniff). I settled on Poweramp, not because it was perfect, but because it was the first one I came to that was good enough. I just want to listen to some music, people, not commit my soul to a single, ringing, crystalline-pure music player that rules them all. Sheesh.

Someday I may do a better review, too. All of the usual things about tablets are at worst adequate on the N7.

Oh, one piece of free advice, worth every penny you paid: Don't go hog wild buying really great accessories. Shop around. A $3 wire easel from a craft store will make a fine desk stand. I have one at work and one at home. A chopstick and a binder clip will do in a pinch. Also, there are good $10 EVA zip cases that will protect your N7 for transport. They don't have to be purpose built. My old K3 had a case that loosely fits the N7 (freebie!) and my KPW1 lives in a similar case. As to ear buds, the candy-colored $5 ones in the bin at the cash register at WalGreens are my favorite, and you never misplace them, because candy-colored.
text_fidelity_b: Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black) SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Elite 85h Wireless Noise-Canceling Headphones, Black – Over Ear Bluetooth Headphones Compatible with iPhone and Android - Built-in Microphone, Long Battery Life - Rain and Water Resistant If you’re looking for unmatched sound reproduction in a very quiet music room, neither the Bose 35 nor the Jabra 85h is competing in that studio monitor class.

These are yeoman everyday transit use with great sound quality. It’s the noise cancelling depth that shuts out the chaos that makes the two exceptional. Ambient sustained engine/crowd noise will wear you out. That’s what makes noise cancelling central for me.

Noise cancelling – Jabra is the first headphone experience every bit the equal with the Bose 35. Other noise reduction players competing in the price bracket don’t come close. The Jabra and Bose cancellation are different. Audible net cancellation is so close to the same that I can’t discriminate. Bose noise cancelling has a sort of over-pressure feeling that I don’t notice in the Jabra. It’s not a discriminator or fatigue element either way for me. If you know what I mean, you will notice it.

Bass – Jabra by a hair

Treble – Jabra wins

Clarity – Bose by a hair

Comfort – High personal importance for air travel. Bose passes the 8-hour flight test. I believe the Jabra will too.

The Jabra 85h is incredibly impressive. It’s a competitive break-through from my perspective. The same price range as Bose 35. Overall the same with very subtle differences that make a winner impossible to my ear. I’d need an acoustics lab to compare the 2 in detail and that degree of detail would be irrelevant for me or the typical user in the price bracket.
Nobody’s going to go wrong with the Jabra 85h. Bose has the first genuine competitor in the price range. That’s good for everybody.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Elite 85h Wireless Noise-Canceling Headphones, Black – Over Ear Bluetooth Headphones Compatible with iPhone and Android - Built-in Microphone, Long Battery Life - Rain and Water Resistant

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Party Speaker - Wireless PA Speaker with Lights, Radio, Bass Boost, Mic Input and USB Charging ***Updated** 8/13/2019

This speaker was plugged in and fully charged after receiving. I have not been able to get it to charge since. Even when plugged in it turns on, says low battery then immediately turns off.

I removed battery to manually charge (there is a compartment under the speaker). Once removed from charger at 26v, as soon as it was connected to the stereo, voltage dropped to 10v, said low battery again and shut off. This speaker went straight to the trash. I had higher hopes for this speaker. Unfortunately it didn’t last longer than a couple of weeks.

For the size of this speaker, I was expecting much better sound.

With the bass button on, the sound is fairly clear and sounds ok. Bass doesn’t hit as hard as I thought it would. I have another speaker half the size that sounds better than this one (at half the price). Without the bass button turned on, the sound is much lower and no longer allows an equalizer setting to be selected.

To turn on, press and hold power button. BT setup was easy and device will automatically connect to the last paired device upon turning on.

Once charged, this is a wireless speaker. It can be paired to another identical speaker. I don’t need 2 of these so I won’t be doing that. It would be nice if it could be paired to any other BT capable speaker.

There are handles on the sides to make carrying easy.

USB port is convenient for charging your phone or other mp3 device. Microphone port works fine and has its own volume knob.

The light on the speaker isn’t super bright but is annoying during daylight hours. It comes on automatically after the bass button is pressed and has to be manually shut off by pressing the light button 7-8 times (it has to go through each of the light settings before turning off).

This would be alright as a garage speaker or even as a kids karaoke machine but It isn’t something I would want to carry around to parties, nor is the sound something to show off.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Party Speaker - Wireless PA Speaker with Lights, Radio, Bass Boost, Mic Input and USB Charging

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW This is my second SSD, my first being a Kingston (with the Taiwan firmware thank God) so I thought install was going to be fairly easy; it was not. My system (Win7) did not recognize the drive, but the included software, Samsung Magician, said the drive was there, operating properly, but was "frozen". I googled the malfunction and found out that the drive had no partitions.

So first step was to get in Disk Management, find the drive, click on the 113+gb unallocated space and create a partition.

Step two, reboot and change my boot sequence because Samsung Magician felt it was necessary to change it for me and made this new SSD my boot drive, even though it had no OS on it to boot.

Step three, change my power management plan back to what I had before because Samsung Magician felt it was better to change it to hibernate instead of what I wanted. I hate Hibernate.

After that it worked great. I use this SSD for games only because it's so damn fast, but I wish the included software and instructions were better, hence the 4 stars and not 5.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW

With it, I can easily verify whether a given charger is actually outputting the advertised power. So far I've tried it on an Anker 65W charger and an Apple 96W charger connected to a MacBook Pro and both times the cable LED agreed with the charger's ratings. This cable will come in handy when I occasionally need to charge with strange/no-name chargers or built-in USB plugs at some hotels.

The cable is pretty long - 10' as the product description indicates - and also a bit stiffer than I expected. For now I feel uncomfortable wrapping it around my hand into a ring as I usually do with cables, especially since the cable came folded and it's hard to get rid of the creases. Included on the cable is a velcro strap that makes keeping things tidy either way.

I think this is a very useful cable - especially the addition of the LED will make it a companion in my travels. I recommend it.

Wall Outlet Extender Surge Protector - 6 Outlet Wall Adapter with 3 USB Charging Ports (1 USB-C, 2 USB A), Multi Plug Outlets Wall Mount with Top Phone Holder for Home, Dorm Essentail, 490 Joules There has been an unpleasant shift, from who is responsible for supplying the power adapters for USB powered appliances. And, for the number of simple household appliances that now require those adapters. I suppose that I can see the logic in it. Newer electrical devices now require lower power. Thence, adapters. At first, they came with the device, like cell phones were supplied with the wall adapters. Eventually, you had to buy your own adapters. Even now, you have to be careful in selecting an adapter. There are basic ones that only have 3 amps. Some have 5 amps or more. Some only split all their power between multiple ports. Some are 'smart' and provide all the amps needed to multiple devices. Now, that's pretty much the rule. You gotta do it yourself and you better know what you're looking for. Disappointment is more common than satisfaction, in this new game.

These outlet adapters from Mifusa probably wouldn't have been my optimum choice, had the listing been a little more informative. But, based on what I read and how it works, it will do well enough.

The six outlets are too close together for bulky plugs or those that have the transformers built into the plugs. The total amperage across all three USB ports is only 3 amps. So, don't look to power multiple USB devices efficiently. BUT, you CAN plug six AC (that's alternating current, not air conditioning) of a low enough power draw, and three USB powered devices, IF they will all fit in the MIFUSA device, and know that they also have surge protection, as indicated by the little green light.

One star being crap and five stars being spectacular, I rate these as being 'okay'.
text_fidelity_b: Wall Outlet Extender Surge Protector - 6 Outlet Wall Adapter with 3 USB Charging Ports (1 USB-C, 2 USB A), Multi Plug Outlets Wall Mount with Top Phone Holder for Home, Dorm Essentail, 490 Joules

It will also be good for using with my projector, as its sound is not very loud. I tried listening to music on it from my phone first, and it sounds pretty good, though it could use more bass, especially for music.
Maybe, it's because I grew up in the 80s era, when there was real music and it had lots of bass, and I still want a lot of it. This speaker just doesn't have quite enough for me, but I still really like it. It is a bit taller and skinnier than a couple of older echo dots, and it doesn't have the same exact quality of sound, but sounds pretty darn good.
The color-changing light effect is pretty cool, but I wish there was a way to turn it off sometimes. Because I'm using it as a computer speaker most of the day, and it's a bit bothersome.
This little speaker packs a pretty good punch, aside from needing a bit more bass, and not being able to turn the light off. It will work great for times when you need a pretty loud sound source and have little room for a big speaker. It's small, has a slot for an SD card for playing your own playlist, it's rechargeable, and lasts for a good while before needing to be recharged. I would definitely recommend it!
text_fidelity_b: DUOTEN IPX7 Waterproof Speaker, Portable Bluetooth 5.0 Wireless Speaker with Suction Cup Shower Speaker, Longer Playtime RGB Lights, 360° Surround Sound Rich Bass for Outdoors, Travel, Pool, Beach

Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) I bought this to take on a trip. I am traveling very lightly, and I do not like waiting around. I have a smartphone, but it's getting harder for me to read on it. I have an iPad Air, but even that can be a little big on a cramped plane ride.

Plus, I sold my other seven inch tablets (a Galaxy and a MeMo), and I miss them. They're the perfect size for reading. This tablet is so much nicer than what I would have been willing to deal with for fifty bucks. However, there are a couple of issues that keep this from being a five star device, even at this price.

The first is that using an sd card to hold content is no easier than it is with the older tech media players I have spent a fair amount of time trying to figure out. If you can download it to your computer, you can put it on the card and then load the card into the Kindle, but the Kindle doesn't treat the card like a drive that you can save to. A firmware update could fix this.

The second is the weight. I'm actually not sure how I feel about this one. It's definitely heavier than I expected. But it feels solid. So, maybe I like it?

Everything else is great for what I am using it for. Reading books. Very light web browsing. Playing with my FireTV. Buying music to play on the Echo. In other words, it's a great tool for accessing the Amazonverse. As a regular tablet? Good for the price.
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

TP-Link AC750 Wifi Range Extender | Up to 750Mbps | Dual Band WiFi Extender, Repeater, Wifi Signal Booster, Access Point| Easy Set-Up | Extends Wifi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices (RE200) This review is for the TP-link AC750 Dual Band WiFi Range Extender

I am using this on a network that has a Mac Mini, a couple of iPhones and an iPad. None of these devices could print to both printers; it was one or the other and not both on every single Apple product. After trying everything I could think of, I bought this extender and tried to set it up using the Quick Setup instructions. Anyone EVER had the experience of those Quick Setups working? I haven't and I've been using this stuff for decades. After Quick Setup failed to do anything other than connect to my router and open my network up to anyone that could get signal, I tried a different approach.

The EASIEST WAY TO SET THIS UP is to use the WPS button on your router and on the device. Press the WPS button on the router, then, press the WPS button on the extender. After a minute or so, the router and extender are paired/connected and the result is a secure connection to the router (uses the router's password--you do have a password don't you) with a much stronger signal in what were dead zones. Placement of the extender is sort of an experiment and moving it from plug to plug will show you the best location. Moving the extender after pairing does NOT foul up the connection.

I have two printers, a Samsung M2070W laser and an Epson Eco Tank inkjet. Both have wireless capability and can use WPS setup. To setup other WPS capable devices, just press the WPS button on the ROUTER and then the WPS button on the next device you want to connect. The connection to the router goes through the connected extender with no problem and does not interfere with the router/extender pairing. Do each device one at a time.

This was the solution I needed and now all wireless devices work together. It's a neat solution to solving signal strength and connectivity that can be an enormous hassle when using multiple devices from different makers.
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link AC750 Wifi Range Extender | Up to 750Mbps | Dual Band WiFi Extender, Repeater, Wifi Signal Booster, Access Point| Easy Set-Up | Extends Wifi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices (RE200)

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz Delta Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones w/Microphone in Ear Bass All Metal Buds (OldSNM) This is one of those earphones where nearly every piece of praise has to be qualified with “for the price.” But that’s not a bad thing. I like and appreciate high-end earphones but I won’t take a pricey set with me to the gym since there’s a good chance it will get broken or lost. At the same time, I don’t want to listen to the rough sound that the $10 or so buds produce.

This is a great compromise. They sound far better than you would expect give the price but they are no so pricey that it would be a tragedy if they get dropped and mashed by a treadmill (which has happened to me), dropped in the pool (also happened to me) or left behind/stolen (fortunately, not happened to me as of yet).

The build quality is pretty good for the price. The cables are on the thin side, but well-anchored. The 3.5mm plug is angled which makes it easier to plug in, and also keeps it from sticking out too much on an mp3 player. It does not come with a case or any extras other than a set of various sizes of tips.

Comfort is a feature that does not have to be qualified by price – these fit very well and are so lightweight that I don’t even notice that they are on. The set includes a variety of tips to customize the fit to your ear. Since bass response is partially dependent on a good ear fit, you’ll want to experiment with the various sizes of tips to see which offer the best feel and bass response.

The sound clarity is quite good at low to mid volumes. They get rather harsh at louder volumes – these are not earbuds that like to get pushed much beyond a middle of the road volume setting. But while they are in their comfort zone in terms of volume, the sound is clear. The bass response won't shake your skull, but it's decent. Sound isolation is also pretty good.

These won’t thrill you with superlative sound, elegant design or impressive looks, but their performance and build quality are impressive for the price point, and much better than the typical low-end earbuds. Well worth considering if you’re looking for an inexpensive pair of earphones.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz Delta Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones w/Microphone in Ear Bass All Metal Buds (OldSNM)

Shure AONIC 215 Wired Sound Isolating Earbuds, Clear Sound, Single Driver, Secure In-Ear Fit, Detachable Cable, Durable Quality, Compatible with Apple & Android Devices - Blue These sound great. I don't have golden ears, but I believe I can at least partly tell the difference between good and bad headphones/earbud. I loved my last pair, sony buds that I only replaced because the cord finally gave in after probably 6 or 7 years.

The complaints about putting these in are founded, but honestly, if you spend a little time practising, it's not complicated and you can find easier ways. Sometimes I'll put the cord over the ear first, then fold the bud into the canal. Other time, the opposite. I tug on my lobe with the thumb and ring finger and use my index finger to apply pressure on the body of the plug to seat it in my canal.

I do run with these in. They block a lot of sound, but not everything. I' pretty hyper vigilant about my surrounding when I'm running, so I'm usually very aware anyway. I wear them to listen to music while working in the workshop and it turned the quite loud combination of my radial arm saw + shop vac into an EXTREMELY manageable background sound, and I could still hear my son yell at me to shut it off when he wanted to ride his bike in the garage - all without taking away too much from the music.

In less than perfect settings, like resting my head against a pillow (or car seat) they do start to hurt a bit after about an hour. General wear, however, hasn't really had that effect.

The cord doesn't tangle remotely as much as my previous pair, but I hope to keep up the habit of winding them and putting them in the pouch that comes with them.
I got the "black", but they are transparent black. I'd rather opaque, but really, it's not a big deal.
I do sometimes wish the distance between the "Y" where the L/R cords connect was a little longer, again, it's not bothered me enough to dock points, really.
I'd actually give a 4.5/5 but don't feel the need to take away an entire star.

(Update)
7 months it made it without a hitch. Then the right side started to flake on me. I have to contort the wire and get lucky to get sound, which usually stays fine until I remove them and have to do it again the nest time I use them. I'll be returning to Shure for a replacement, but I have to say that my previous Sony pair, with near daily use, lasted 6-7 YEARS without issue, so this bothers me. I'm certain Shure will replace at least the cable, otherwise I'd be dropping more than the one star I took off. I'll update if I have other issues with the replacement process or otherwise.
text_fidelity_b: Shure AONIC 215 Wired Sound Isolating Earbuds, Clear Sound, Single Driver, Secure In-Ear Fit, Detachable Cable, Durable Quality, Compatible with Apple & Android Devices - Blue

Reading the reviews I decided on the TCL 55r615. The voice remote on the r617 wasn’t worth the extra fifty bucks, and the voice function is duplicated on the Roku phone app anyway.

I am VERY happy with the TV; Colors and picture are bright and contrast seems excellent. I’ve watched a couple of 4k documentaries and was blown away with the picture. The Roku menu for the streaming channels really is excellent to use: Far “Snappier” and easier to navigate than any other that I’ve used. text_fidelity_a:
Epson E11E221012 ProSense 307 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and EasyView Display - Black I currently use two mobile GPS devices, an iphone 5 and Garmin Vivioactive 2. The Garmin is a slightly older model so you need that chest strap thing to get heart rate, it is probably more accurate, the new Garmins have the wrist pulse monitor. So I was looking for something with the wrist pulse, and something more accurate, as the Garmin credits me with mileage while I am sitting drinking coffee mid-ride at a cafe etc.
So initial appearances are good. The watch is about standard for a chunky men's, maybe the same as a G-Shock for size. The strap has excellent ventilation built in close to the case of the watch, a new feature I have not seen before. The first thing you have to do is charge it up and the cord is generous at a foot or so and it clips very securely to the watch rather than using a magnetic base or anything, these are all very well designed parts.
Ok so here we go with functionality. First off Epson is primarily known as a printer company and perhaps they are attempting to diversify. If it were not for the fact that this was a free product sample, I would never have even considered it, as there are certain brands that are associated with GPS and certain brands that are associated with, well, printers. So next morning after a night of charging there was 1 1/2 hrs of fiddling with this thing before any exercise could be attempted. The watch works off buttons, there is no touchscreen functionality, which other devices achieve at a lower price point. Once you pair with your phone you can make changes, but it might take a while to get to that point. So this watch is set up around runners and walkers. I'm a cyclist, I don't run. To select cycling as my activity of choice is like five button pushes, rather than a single screen with a variety of exercise modes to choose from. It's rather like programming a ... printer. Navigating between menus and functions is slow, and establishing satellite connection for GPS is also protracted.
So we're off; about a dozen miles just to check it out. The ProSense buzzes and lights every mile to let you know you've done a mile. Yes, a mile jogging might be an achievement for me, but I often cycle fifty miles or more and am simply annoyed by all the clamor on my wrist. To be fair, most of these functions are adjustable and turn-offable and all the rest of it, if you don't mind programming a ... printer.
So I'm drinking my coffee at the bike shop and being falsely credited for mileage just like the Garmin but worse. There are some exercise pause features and whatnot on the watch and I'm not sure where I'm at in the laborious settings process but I can tell you that Strava on a phone is all over you, knows the instant you get off the bike. I'm told by geeks that Strava also has better analytics you see, they correct the Garmin's reporting, and maybe this Epson too, things got murky in there. Now to save my activity and transfer it to Strava (it's like a fitness Facebook for those of you who don't know) through paired apps. The Garmin is almost simultaneous to Strava, the Epson took about twenty minutes to get into Strava. Strava gave me 11.7 miles and 711ft of elevation, important to me because I'm in the November climbing challenge, that's 8000 metres, roughly the height of Everest, (I hope to make 50% of the challenge.) The Epson gave me about 2400ft of descending and 1400ft ascending. Is that the length of the road that was sloped? Is the difference between the two my actual gain? That would be 1000ft difference, an error of approx 30%. I'm going to say the Epson was wildly inaccurate on elevation and is more for runners.
Heart Rate. Very good tracking. The watch (viewed through my phone) breaks down cardio into the five zones, and does other stuff the fiends are really into like VO2 whatever that is. So I was very pleased with that aspect, I know my particulars and have little desire to go to zone five which is like 180bpm through 240bpm. I got into zone 2 at under 140bpm and the app said I did very little aerobic work, hey it was just a coffee run.
Battery life, I'll have to go out on an all-dayer and see, but if the watch does 20 or more hours that would be very useful on weekend trips etc.
text_fidelity_b: Epson E11E221012 ProSense 307 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and EasyView Display - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player Picture is nice,

The real reason I'm sending the units (I've had two) back, however, is that the player refuses to output the various high quality audio formats, including 7.1 DTS Master Audio. The digital coax cable barely works and the HDMI 2 audio output simply does not work, Admittedly I have an older receiver -- a Sony STR-DA5400ES, from 2009. But it has multiple HDMI inputs and the HDMI 2 audio output on the X800 is specifically designed to send audio to an older amp. Even Sony phone support says it should work. But it doesn't.. I spent 1 hour and 7 minutes with Sony ES support today going through every possible menu permutation on both the Amp and the UBP-X800 player. No luck The HDMI is dead. Zero output. The coax output can only send DTS EX 5.1, even though the player itself tells me it's playing DTS Master Audio 7.1.

This UBP-X800 has two HDMI outputs: one for video, one for audio. In case you don't have a 4K receiver with the ever-changing HDMI protocols, you're supposed to be able to feed HDMI audio to the amp. So I fed the video directly to the Samsung's video input (a direct cable connection) and another HDMI to my amp.

Zero audio from the player's HDMI audio feed. Not a peep of audio at all.

So I used the orange RCA digital audio coax connector to get surround sound audio.

But the coax digital audio cable only delivers DTS EX 5.1, not the 7.1 DTS Master Audio available on the Kingsman 4K disk. I updated the player's and the TV's firmware and read the manual. Nothing fixes the problem. Using all new, very short, high-speed HDMI 2.0 cables too.

My ancient Sony BDP-S560 Blu-ray player feeds all formats to the same 5400ES amp properly. I get great 7.1 DTS Master HD audio. Thus my old Blu-ray player sounds way better than my brand new advanced Sony UHD player.
Researching at the Sony forum under the UBP-X800 Audio Problems thread, answers were all over the place and none worked, I tried to register so I could post my problem and the website wouldn't allow me to. The comments there were complaining that they could not get the ATMOS tracks working.

I have no choice but to pack both X800s up and send them back.

Eventually I found that I needed to plug the 4K player into input 3 of the TV for the image to stabilize. Interesting that only some inputs on the TV can handle UHD source. But still, the player's audio doesn't work with my Sony Amp (Sony's fault).

HDMI was supposed to solve all these problems, but I suspect the HDCP copy protection schemes are really screwing things up or the firmware has bugs or companies just produce inferior products. Rather disappointing.
text_fidelity_b: Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player

text_fidelity_a:
WiFi Extender Long Range Repeater 300Mbps Router Wireless Access Point Signal Amplifier Booster Complies with 802.11n/g/b with WPS Button,Extends WiFi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices Just got this today because we are having wifi accessibility issues in our upstairs guest bedroom (and every good host knows that if you don't have decent wifi in your guest room, you can expect your guests to leave you a holy mess, in retaliation).

Couldn't believe how easy this is to set up, though! I'm pretty tech-savvy, anyhow (after 2 years of various tech-related military schools). Not that I needed to be! The included instructions are incredibly clear and easy to follow. On the contrary, the last AP/repeater I bought merely schooled me in when it's acceptable to take a hammer to one of these things. (FYI: it's right after you've tried, unsuccessfully, for an hour to get it to connect to your wifi). So I really appreciated how simple and fast this is to set up.

How fast, exactly? It literally took like 2 minutes to set up...and only THAT long because I had to go all the way into the other room and log into my laptop to complete the instructions.

Just a head's up, for the less-tech savvy:

This is NOT a wifi signal amplifier, as such. You WILL be creating a NEW wireless access point (aka wifi log-on)...even if you install this in "repeater" mode--vs. the wired-to-wireless AP (access point) mode.

So, for example, instead of logging into whatever your network is called, when you need to use the wifi that this repeats for you, you'll be logging into a new connection. They call it, by default, "My Repeater" (I assume that is so you'll never forget who actually owns it), but you can rename it to anything you want (mine is henceforth known as Fluffy Gigglebuns). You'll still use the same password as you use for your main connection, though...and therein lies the genius of it. You can make your guests feel special (or, in my case, humiliated) by personalizing the repeater network name, but the password will be the same as it is for whatever network AP you are having it repeat.

Lastly, this does offer an extra feature I think is worth mentioning:

You can also use this as a wireless adapter to connect a multimedia or other tech device that requires or ONLY allows internet connectivity via an ethernet (aka wired) connection.

So if you have something like an older roku, or game console, etc. that can only connect to the internet via an ethernet cable, you can apparently use THIS device to quickly convert it to use your wifi connection.
text_fidelity_b: WiFi Extender Long Range Repeater 300Mbps Router Wireless Access Point Signal Amplifier Booster Complies with 802.11n/g/b with WPS Button,Extends WiFi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices

Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology [[VIDEOID:fab011cbaf4d8ff273fb360a6d075448]] My granddaughter is too young to remember the big bulky Polaroid instant camera, so when I showed her this camera and told her it took instant pictures that she could use as stickers her comment was "AWESOME", and she's dying to get her hands on it. This compact sized 10 megapixel camera offers users the option of printing 2" x 3" photos instantly or adding up to a 32 GB micro SD card in order to store or share images.

The camera is straight forward and simple to use. If you want to take instant photos just load [[ASIN:B00ZSPI3A6 Polaroid 2x3 inch Premium ZINK Photo Paper TWIN PACK (20 Sheets) - Compatible With Polaroid Snap, Z2300, SocialMatic Instant Cameras & Zip Instant Printer]] into the chamber in the back of the camera, remove the magnetic lens cap, and gently press the viewfinder to turn the camera on.

Using the selector wheel at the top left, you can choose to take your photos in color, black & white, or sepia (which is like old time tin type for an antique look). Choose one, and then press the button next to that to select whether you want the photo to have a border or not. You can even press another button on the top to activate a 10 second delay to take selfies, and there's also a "photo booth mode" which takes a series of six quick pictures over the course of 10 seconds that you can set by depressing the shutter for three seconds.

Once you've chosen all of your desired options simply frame your shot in the viewfinder and press the shutter. There's no zoom or available adjustment, the camera automatically focuses and uses flash if needed, and the 2" x 3" print comes out of the side of the camera clear, sharp, and dry to the touch in under a minute. If you have film loaded the camera is going to print photos automatically when you press the shutter, so don't load paper if you prefer to use the micro SD card and not print. The camera has an auto sleep function that will shut it off to save battery power if sufficient times lapses between use, or you can just press the viewfinder back down to shut it off manually.

There are no instructions that comes with the camera, but you can read or print the manual yourself by going to polaroidsnapcamera dot come. You can also find the firmware update there. Be sure to charge the camera fully when you receive it, then insert a Micro SD card and update the firmware before using it. (Available here: http://polaroid.com/products/polaroid-snap-camera) Besides printing paper, you'll definitely want to have a MicroSD card for the camera and a case: [[ASIN:B017A1D6TI Polaroid Neoprene Pouch for The Polaroid Snap Instant Camera (Black)]].

There are several things about this product that could be improved on:
1. No sample printing paper included
2. No picture preview
3. No strap to attach the lens cover to which would help prevent losing it
4. Viewfinder pops open too easily
5. No instruction manual or link mention of the firmware update (or link to it) included with product

Otherwise, the camera is well made and fun to use. I can see where kids would have a lot of fun with this camera, but the photo paper isn't cheap so I may let my granddaughter use some and then just mostly use the Micro SD card. This could also be useful for producing instant photos at special events such as birthday parties, weddings, proms, and for other occasions, and the peel off backing on the photo paper makes it nice for scrap booking.

This instant camera was provided at no cost for my evaluation and review.
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology
